title: Unit 10: Sedimentary Rocks
sub: Reading: pages 134–150  ·  20 points  ·  15 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Answer every question. For multiple choice, circle the single best answer. Write short answers in complete sentences.

choices: the process by which compacted sediments become cemented together into solid rock
the chemical weathering of an exposed rock face
the melting of sediment to form magma
the movement of sediment from the site of erosion to the site of deposition
questions.why: p. 135 — it happens at depths of hundreds to thousands of meters and involves two steps: compaction from burial, then cementation as minerals crystallize in the pores between clasts.

questions.stem: Most sand-sized clasts are made of quartz because
choices: quartz dissolves readily and reprecipitates as sand
sand can only form from igneous rock
quartz is the only mineral that breaks into sand-sized pieces
quartz is more resistant to weathering than any other common mineral
questions.why: p. 135 — by contrast, most clasts smaller than sand are clay minerals, and most clasts larger than sand are actual fragments of rock.

questions.stem: A clastic sedimentary rock dominated by rounded clasts larger than 2 mm is
choices: conglomerate
arkose
shale
breccia
questions.why: p. 140 — breccia has angular clasts. Conglomerates form in high-energy settings such as fast-flowing rivers where particles get rounded; breccias form where particles were not carried far, such as alluvial fans and talus slopes.

questions.stem: By far the most common chemical sedimentary rock is
choices: Chert
Limestone
Halite
Banded iron formation
questions.why: p. 141 — almost all limestone forms in the oceans, mostly on shallow continental shelves in tropical regions with coral reefs.

questions.stem: As an inland sea in an arid region evaporates, which of these precipitates last?
choices: Carbonates, at about 50% of the original volume
Gypsum, at about 20% of the original volume
Halite, at about 10% of the original volume
They all precipitate at the same time
questions.why: p. 143 — the order follows how concentrated the remaining water has become, so halite requires the most evaporation.

questions.stem: Cross-bedding is especially valuable to geologists because it
choices: contains more fossils than any other structure
records the direction of current or wind flow at the time of deposition
proves a rock is chemical rather than clastic
gives the exact numerical age of the rock
questions.why: pp. 145–146 — analyzed in detail it can also indicate the rate of flow and the amount of sediment available. Ripples help the same way, since their steepest face points downflow.

questions.stem: The principle of inclusions states that rock fragments within a sedimentary layer must be older than the layer itself.
questions.why: p. 144 — the cobbles inside a conglomerate had to exist before the conglomerate could form around them.

questions.stem: Most fossils are found in igneous rock.
questions.why: Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock. Some occur in metamorphic rock, but fossils are rare in igneous rock because it forms from flowing molten material. (p. 147)

questions.stem: Explain the difference between clastic and chemical sedimentary rocks, and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Clastic rocks are made of material transported as solid fragments (clasts); chemical rocks are made of material transported as ions dissolved in solution.
questions.rubric: 1 pt clastic defined — composed mainly of material carried as solid fragments; examples include mudstone, shale, sandstone, conglomerate, breccia, and coal. 1 pt chemical defined — composed mainly of material carried as ions in solution (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, HCO₃⁻); examples include limestone, chert, banded iron formation, gypsum, and halite. 1 pt for one valid example of each. Bonus insight: the two overlap, since nearly all clastic rocks are cemented by minerals precipitated from dissolved ions. (pp. 135 and 141)

questions.stem: Banded iron formations record a major change in Earth’s atmosphere. Explain what that change was, and why these rocks essentially stopped forming after about 1800 Ma.
questions.answer: They record the rise of free oxygen produced by photosynthetic bacteria, which converted dissolved iron in seawater into insoluble iron oxide that sank to the seafloor. They stopped forming when the oceans ran out of dissolved iron.
questions.rubric: 1 pt — photosynthetic bacteria such as cyanobacteria evolved around 3500 Ma and consumed carbon dioxide to produce oxygen, but for about a billion years that oxygen was consumed by other processes; free oxygen began accumulating around 2400 Ma. 1 pt — over roughly 600 million years that oxygen converted soluble ferrous iron to insoluble ferric iron, forming hematite that settled onto the deep seafloor as BIF. 1 pt — by 1800 Ma little dissolved iron remained in the oceans, so BIF formation essentially stopped. (p. 143)
